prompt: According to the lesson, why do experienced people still decide badly without data?
hint: Compare what memory keeps with what the records keep.

choices.text: They rarely take the time to look carefully
choices.why: The lesson says most of them do look; effort is not the problem.

choices.text: What they have seen is a biased sample of what happened
choices.why: Right: memory keeps the vivid, the loud and the recent, so experience is a skewed sample.

choices.text: Their experience comes from a different company and does not transfer to this one
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so: Helena's experience is of Varanda itself, and it still misleads.

choices.text: Senior people are wrong more often than junior ones
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: they are right often, which is how they became senior.

prompt: Match each situation at Varanda to the way experience misleads.
hint: Vivid, loud, recent, and the person at the top.

pairs.left: Caio is sure Juiz de Fora deliveries are late because of two bad complaints
The manager who phones every week gets his problems fixed first
A weak October makes everybody worried about the online shop
pairs.right: The last month stands in for the year

pairs.left: The meeting ends when the CEO says what she thinks

prompt: Caio remembered Juiz de Fora as the town where deliveries are always late. What did the records say?
hint: Two percentages, close together.

choices.text: Its late rate was about twice the company's
choices.why: That is what Caio's memory suggested; the records did not bear it out.

choices.text: It had no late deliveries at all in 2025
choices.why: There were late deliveries there, as everywhere; the point is how many.

choices.text: 6.8% late against 6.5% across every route
choices.why: Right: close to the average. Two vivid complaints made an ordinary route feel like the worst.

choices.text: The records were too incomplete to say anything
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says the delivery records were incomplete.

prompt: What does the lesson say BI is for when the CEO already holds a strong opinion?
hint: Helena asked for the analysis herself.

choices.text: To prove the senior person wrong in front of the board
choices.why: Helena is not a villain here, and an analysis written to win an argument stops being trusted.

choices.text: To replace the decision with whatever the table says
choices.why: The last section of the lesson says the data narrows the decision and does not take it.

choices.text: To stay silent, because experience beats a spreadsheet
choices.why: The lesson says decisions go wrong when they use only one of the two.

choices.text: To give her the part of the picture memory cannot hold: every store, counted the same way
choices.why: Right: experience says which questions matter; data says how often and how big.

prompt: Which three things does the lesson say every decision has? Choose all that apply.
hint: Without them, Lívia is not looking at a decision yet.

choices.text: At least two options, doing nothing included
choices.why: Right: "enlarge Contagem" alone is not a decision.

choices.text: A dashboard to present the answer
choices.why: The form of the answer comes later and depends on the question.

choices.text: A deadline after which the answer is no use
choices.why: Right: the budget is approved in April, so a May answer changes nothing.

choices.text: A cost of picking the worse option
choices.why: Right: R$ 4 million for a store, a few thousand reais for cushions.

choices.text: A year of history in the data
choices.why: Some decisions have no history at all, and they are still decisions.

prompt: Sônia asks for 2025 sick-leave days broken down by day of the week, "to see". Why did Lívia not build it?
hint: Ask what would be done with the answer.

choices.text: No result would have changed anything Sônia does
choices.why: Right: the policy is fixed by law and the union agreement, so the analysis had nothing to change.

choices.text: Sick-leave data is personal, so HR questions are off limits to BI
choices.why: Personal data needs care, not a ban, and that was not Lívia's reason here.

choices.text: Two days of work is too long for any single request
choices.why: Two days would be cheap for a decision worth millions; cost is weighed against what the answer can change.

choices.text: A manager's request goes after the CEO's
choices.why: Rank was not the test; Helena's request passed because an answer could change it.

prompt: Varanda will order 200 extra cushions this month whatever the data says, because the supplier's minimum is 200. How much is an analysis of cushion colours worth for this order?
hint: Could any answer change the choice?

choices.text: A lot, because more data makes any decision better
choices.why: Data is worth what it can change; more of it changes nothing here.

choices.text: It depends on how carefully the chart is drawn
choices.why: Presentation cannot add value to an answer that changes no choice.

choices.text: About R$ 4 million, the cost of a wrong decision
choices.why: That is the store enlargement; the cushion order costs a few thousand reais.

choices.text: Little, unless the colours are still open
choices.why: Right: the quantity is fixed, so only a choice still open — such as the colours — could make the analysis worth doing.

prompt: By the lesson's rough rule, the value of an answer grows with what a wrong choice would lose and with the chance it changes the choice, and shrinks with the ___ of getting it.
hint: An afternoon against R$ 4 million.

prompt: In your sheet, what are Contagem's 2025 sales per square metre, in reais?
What is the chain's sales per square metre for the nine stores together, in reais, computed as the lesson does in D11?
hint: Divide the two totals, then round.

prompt: Why does D11 divide total sales by total floor instead of averaging the nine values in column D?
hint: Nova Lima has 1,500 m² and Contagem 3,200.

choices.text: The AVERAGE function is not available in every spreadsheet
choices.why: AVERAGE exists in all three spreadsheets the course uses; the reason is what the number means.

choices.text: An average of the nine would weigh a small store the same as a large one
choices.why: Right: the chain's figure is reais per metre over all its metres, so each store counts by its size.

choices.text: Dividing the totals gives a rounder number
choices.why: Roundness is not a reason; 4,019 is not round.

choices.text: The two methods give the same result, and division is faster to type
choices.why: They give different results whenever stores differ in size, which they do.

prompt: Contagem has 1.8 times Savassi's floor and sells 1.05 times as much. What does that say about Helena's reason for enlarging it?
hint: What is "sells the most" mostly a statement about?

choices.text: Contagem is a badly run store and its manager should be replaced
choices.why: The lesson says the ranking does not say Contagem is a bad store; it sits near the chain's average.

choices.text: Selling the most is mostly a consequence of being the largest
choices.why: Right: per square metre it is fourth, at 59% of Savassi.

choices.text: Contagem should be enlarged even more, since it is already the biggest
choices.why: Size is what explains its sales, so it is not evidence that more size would sell well.

choices.text: Nothing: total sales are the right measure for this decision
choices.why: The decision is about adding floor, so sales relative to floor is the closer measure.

prompt: Put these four stores in order of 2025 sales per square metre, highest first.
hint: Divide sales by floor for each.
trap: Ordering by total sales puts Contagem first and Nova Lima last of the four, which is the ranking the lesson takes apart.

prompt: Nova Lima sells R$ 6,300 per square metre. Why does the lesson say this does not tell Helena what an enlargement there would sell?
hint: Metre 1,501.

choices.text: Because the figure is rounded to whole reais
choices.why: Rounding moves it by less than a real; the problem is what kind of number it is.

choices.text: Because 2025 was an unusual year for the chain
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says 2025 was unusual.

choices.text: It is an average, and new metres sell what the extra space attracts
choices.why: Right: the table measures the metres that exist, not the next one.

choices.text: Because Nova Lima's floor area is measured differently from the others
choices.why: The lesson gives no reason to doubt the floor areas.

prompt: In 2021 Varanda closed a 3,000 m² store that never covered its costs. Why does that matter to an analysis of today's nine stores?
hint: Which stores leave a row in this year's data?

choices.text: The data holds only survivors, so large stores look safer than they were
choices.why: Right: that is survivorship, and the closed store is the counter-example the table cannot show.

choices.text: Its old sales are still mixed into the 2025 totals and inflate the large stores
choices.why: A store closed in 2021 has no sales in 2025; that absence is the issue.

choices.text: It shows that Contagem will close if it is enlarged
choices.why: One closed store is a warning about large stores, not a prediction about one store.

choices.text: It does not matter; closed stores are irrelevant to new decisions
choices.why: They are some of the most relevant evidence a decision about store size has.

prompt: The lesson prefers "data-___" to "data-driven": the numbers are one input, weighed by somebody accountable for the choice.
hint: The numbers are an input; a person decides.

prompt: Lívia's ranking is by sales per square metre. Which missing number could reorder it, according to the lesson?
hint: What Helena actually cares about, and Savassi's neighbourhood.

choices.text: Each store's number of employees
choices.why: Staff costs matter to profit, but the lesson names rent, the cost that differs most by location.

choices.text: Each store's rent
choices.why: Right: Savassi has the highest rent per metre, so the best seller per metre may not be the most profitable.

choices.text: The online shop's sales
choices.why: The online shop has no floor to enlarge, which is why it was left out.

choices.text: The number of Saturday visitors to each store
choices.why: That brings back Helena's busiest-hour view; it says nothing about profit.

pairs.right: What metre 1,501 in Nova Lima would sell
Varanda has never enlarged a store

prompt: Renata says the online shop had a terrible October and wants to cut its 2026 budget. What is the first thing this lesson would have Lívia point out?
hint: How much of a year is one month?

choices.text: That the online shop sells more than any single store, so it cannot be cut
choices.why: Size is not the argument; the evidence for the cut is what is weak.

choices.text: That one month is a poor stand-in for a year
choices.why: Right: the last month standing in for the year is one of the three ways experience misleads.

choices.text: That October always falls
choices.why: Nothing in this lesson says so, and lesson 7 is where an October is diagnosed.

choices.text: That a marketing director's view counts less than the CEO's
choices.why: Rank does not settle anything; the HiPPO is the problem the lesson names, not a rule.

prompt: Put Lívia's handling of Helena's store question in the order the lesson tells it.
hint: The test comes before the sheet.
items: Check that an answer could change the choice
Divide each store's sales by its floor
Send the two rankings with their limits written down
Helena asks for other stores to be costed
trap: Starting with the sheet skips the test that decides whether the sheet is worth building.

prompt: Contagem's sales per square metre are what percentage of Savassi's, rounded to a whole number?
hint: =ROUND(D4/D2*100,0) on the store sheet

prompt: Varanda considers opening its first store in São Paulo, and a director asks for "the data that proves it will work". By this lesson, what is the honest reply?
hint: What history does a first store have?

choices.text: Rank São Paulo against the nine stores by sales per square metre
choices.why: A store that does not exist has no row to rank.

choices.text: Refuse, since data has nothing to say about something new
choices.why: The data covers the neighbourhood of the decision — the stores Varanda has — and that is worth showing, with its limit.

choices.text: Show what the existing stores say, and state plainly that no data covers a first store in a new city
choices.why: Right: new things have no history, so the analysis informs the decision and judgement carries the rest.

choices.text: Build a forecast from the nine stores and present it as the answer
choices.why: The lesson calls that a guess with arithmetic around it, unless its limits are stated.
